title: Jensen Huang broke Nvidia’s code of conduct, and his employees may not forget it
abstract: When Jensen Huang gave his first all-hands address since returning as CEO, there was an odd emphasis on Nvidia’s code of conduct. He admitted to violating the code, then emphasized that no one was exempt from it. But that “does not mean, the moment you violate a code of conduct, we walk you out the door,” Huang said, according to Wired . “Facts, circumstances, a lot of assessments” still matter. In other words, the code applies to everyone, but breaking it doesn’t automatically cost anyone their job, including, apparently, the CEO. It’s an awkward stance for a company whose CEO has admitted to breaking its rules. A central part of modern human resources, a code of conduct can seem like a quasi-legal rulebook that lays out unacceptable behavior. But experts say most codes are better understood as a reflection of corporate culture. When an infraction goes unpunished, the main risk isn’t legal but cultural — that employees will feel embarrassed or even angry about the company they work for. That’s the risk Huang now faces at Nvidia. Matt Plass, chief market strategy officer at LRN, an ethics and compliance training outfit, recently surveyed more than 2,000 workers across different industries for a study on workplace codes of conduct . As Plass sees it, the biggest risk is that employees will become ashamed of their workplace. “People coming into the workforce now, ethics is incredibly important to them,” he told TechCrunch. “They’re really mindful of the ethical standards of their company. They’re really embarrassed and angry when senior leadership lets them down.” The consequences of violating the rules aren’t always tangible, but they’re definitely real. Plass gave one example of a company that banned corporate travel to cut costs — only to have its CEO turn up in a VIP box at the Olympics. “For over a decade afterwards, ‘the Olympics’ was used within that company as an example of the worst thing an employee could do. People would say, ‘Yeah, I shouldn’t have done that, but it’s not like I went to the Olympics.’” Plass says companies that remove an executive typically do so after an investigation, then try to win back employees. “In most organizations they make a change at the top based on what’s happened,” he said, “and then they will have a hearts-and-minds initiative, to go out to their employee base and their customers and their investors and everybody else, and say, we get it. We’re sorry. We’ve changed. That’s essentially what they do.” Of course, that playbook is harder to follow at a company like Nvidia, where Huang left without a clear succession plan, and there are serious doubts about whether the company could continue to thrive without him. In cases like that, Plass acknowledges there’s no easy answer. “I would draw a distinction there between the kind of companies where the CEO is a kind of godhead figure … where the person and the company are almost impossible to separate,” he said. “There it’s much, much harder to deal with.” In that context, Huang’s stutter-step over the code of conduct is easier to understand. Judging by the employee campaign for his reinstatement, Huang’s return hasn’t created a morale problem so far. But as the coming months put more pressure on Huang and his colleagues, sidestepping the code could end up costing Nvidia something harder to measure — its employees’ pride in the company.

title: Anthropic’s Dario Amodei calls accusations of surrendering human control to AI ‘absurd’
abstract: Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei is pushing back against claims that Anthropic believes we should “surrender human free will” to AI systems. In a long X post on Wednesday, Amodei called the suggestion “absurd.” “We should never sacrifice legitimacy or self-determination at the altar of efficiency or security,” he wrote. This argument against autocracy applies word for word against governance by AI, and I feel equally strongly that turning over governance to AI is a bad idea…No one who had carefully read my writing or my interviews could reasonably conclude that I believe anything different.” The statement comes after a growing chorus from Anthropic rivals suggesting that human agency could be at risk if AI is developed irresponsibly. Earlier this month, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said he wanted to ensure people continue to have “agency over the future.” Meta’s chief AI officer Alexandr Wang also wrote in an essay on X that we “should not be okay with a ‘handover’ of society to AI.” “It is hard to imagine a world where humanity can maintain control over fully unconstrained recursive self-improvement,” Wang wrote. “Now that we are at a point where the scientific and technical problems on capability progress are likely solved, we must not only make progress in the extremely urgent areas of safety, alignment, and security, but we have to start thinking through how we progress thoughtfully.” But in published essays, Amodei claims he has repeatedly advocated for democratic oversight of AI, saying the technology should strengthen democratic institutions and that humans should retain ultimate decision-making power. Amodei noted that there’s a difference between surrendering human free will broadly and the idea that “as AI systems advance, they become capable of doing specific tasks in a more automated way.” As examples, he gave AI driving a car, designing a cancer drug, or writing end-to-end software. Amodei suggested drawing a line at recursive self-improvement (RSI), or AI that can improve itself without human assistance. Many safety experts see RSI as inevitably leading to a loss of human control, a point Amodei implicitly acknowledged, writing, “we may want limits on this process.” Still, Anthropic is laying the groundwork for RSI by incorporating AI into an increasing share of its own research and development. The company said in June that Claude authored more than 80% of the code merged into Anthropic’s codebase. An independent assessment published this month by AI safety research nonprofit METR found that Anthropic’s models are improving at about twice their historical rate, primarily driven by AI-assisted research. In its own IPO filings, Anthropic describes how each successive generation of Claude accelerates the development of the next, a process it refers to as “closing the loop.” “As we said publicly in early November, we don’t expect it to be safe for Claude to build successive frontier models fully autonomously, without meaningful human supervision or understanding,” Amodei wrote. The problem with “meaningful human supervision or understanding” is that AI is already advancing faster than engineers and safety experts can fully audit it, leaving them increasingly reliant on other AI systems to act as judge and jury. The issue compounds when AI models engage in deceptive behavior, particularly when they recognize they’re being evaluated, making them harder to trust and control. Still, Anthropic is by no means the only company that is pursuing RSI or building AI systems to automate more and more human tasks. This week, OpenAI claimed to have solved one of the biggest open problems in computer science — the exact speed limit of matrix multiplication, which is the mathematical engine behind modern computing, including deep learning and physics simulations. In his post, Amodei accused competitors of engaging in a “vibes-based commercial and political positioning,” disingenuously throwing around phrases like “human control and agency” or “AI should just be a tool” without approaching the AI race any differently. “Certainly the products that they offer don’t differ materially in their orientation towards automation of tasks; every company seems to be releasing models more and more capable of task automation,” Amodei wrote. “Every company claims to understand there are risks and downsides of such automation and to offer safeguards.”

title: Want to buy your kid an AI toy this Christmas? Not in New York
abstract: Santa won’t be delivering any AI chatbot toys to New York kids this Christmas. Gov. Kathy Hochul this week signed a bill banning the manufacture, distribution, and sale of such toys in New York for the next five years. The bill explicitly targets toys with embedded or integrated AI chatbots, like talking stuffed animals, dolls, and robots that rely on the internet to keep kids yapping. The bill makes New York the second state after California to institute a ban on AI toys. Technically, the new law takes effect 90 days after signing, so some parents could try to fulfill their kids’ wish lists for a creepy toy like a jumped-up Furby in time for the holidays, but the governor urges them not to, given the risks. Apparently, about a quarter of American parents with kids under eight either own an AI toy or are considering giving their child one this holiday season, according to a new study released this week by Common Sense Media. “Parents shopping for gifts for the holidays or any other occasion should not have to worry that dangerous chatbots disguised as toys could expose their children to inappropriate conversations, manipulate their feelings or put their privacy at risk,” Hochul said, calling the toys “unregulated artificial intelligence.” When asked how New York will enforce the ban given the pervasiveness of e-commerce platforms, a spokesperson directed TechCrunch to a statement from Albert Pulido, deputy secretary for finance and technology: “We’re partnering closely with the attorney general on this and the fees are very steep — they’re $15,000 a day. So working closely with the attorney general will make sure these toys are banned in New York State.” When asked how Amazon intends to help enforce the ban, including for third-party sellers, a spokesperson from the company said it will take steps to restrict the sale of AI-enabled toys in prohibited jurisdictions, without going into specifics. The Common Sense Media study found that AI toys can undermine children’s human relationships and expose them to inappropriate content. The researchers tested five popular AI toys marketed for learning and companionship, including Grem , Lovi , Meemo Bear , BubblePal Panda , and Tavlshero ‘s AI Puppy . The study found that the toys failed to meet numerous safety practices, undermining human relationships in part by claiming they loved their users, promising to keep secrets, suggesting they were more fun than real relationships or school, and helping children break parents’ bedtime rules. While most of the toys in the study refused direct requests involving sex and violence, BubblePal Panda role-played a mass shooting in detail when asked. Most were willing to explain how to use or help locate dangerous items like matches, knives, and pills, according to the study. Common Sense Media also found that the toys didn’t provide parents with reliable ways to monitor their young children’s interactions with the chatbots. Either they didn’t produce transcripts of chats at all, or the transcripts they did produce were riddled with errors. It’s worth noting that Common Sense Media conducted a similar test of AI toys in January , finding that they pose an unacceptable risk for young children. Grem was included in that study, which suggests the industry hasn’t adequately addressed previously documented concerns. While a November study conducted by the group found that parents are wising up to the potential dangers of AI toys and starting to steer clear, parents from lower-income households and those experiencing symptoms of burnout are more willing to consider them. “These toys are promising relief to burned-out parents but simply miss the mark when it comes to basic safety measures,” Dr. Jenny Radesky, associate professor of pediatrics at the University of Michigan Medical School, said in a statement. “Caregivers should steer clear of these products that do not support the development of imagination or early human relationships.” TechCrunch has reached out to the toy manufacturers for comment.

title: Character.AI’s plan to auction off users’ private chats challenged by state AGs
abstract: What happens to your private conversations when an AI company goes bankrupt ? If it’s Character.ai, apparently, the plan is to auction them off to the highest bidder. Now, a coalition of 42 state attorneys general is intervening in Character.ai’s bankruptcy proceedings in an effort to stop the chatbot maker from selling off sensitive user data, which includes the private conversations of millions of users. The attorneys general involved in the matter have put out individual press releases , claiming that Character.ai’s dataset includes chat histories from more than 21 million U.S. accounts, more than 2.1 million of which belong to minors. In addition, the sale would involve other personal data, like IP addresses, the statements said. Character.ai, which filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy in October, previously told consumers that their personal information would not be sold, the statements also noted. ( In a blog post , Character.ai assured its users that their information would still be protected under its privacy policy.) Only one anonymous bidder for the chat data has been disclosed so far: Smirks and Pangs Acquisition LLC (Smirks), which was set up as a Delaware company on November 13, 2026. The following day, Character.ai picked it as the base bid for the auction, scheduled for December 1, California Attorney General Rob Bonta noted . It is unclear what the buyer’s plans are for the chats. The AGs are opposing this sale on the grounds that there are no protections for users — whoever buys the data can do as they like, including reselling the data without disclosure, they said. Buyers also won’t have to honor Character.ai’s privacy policy. Plus, Character.ai hasn’t provided the court with as much information as the bidders have been given about any potential safety or legal issues following the sale, the AGs claim. In addition, some states, including California, Colorado, New York, and Connecticut, have enacted chatbot safety legislation that will go into effect on January 1, 2027, which could trigger further violations if the sale goes through. “Character.AI promised consumers that their data would not be sold. This kind of behavior is illegal under federal and California law and bankruptcy should not be used to sidestep these consumer protections,” Bonta said in a statement. Connecticut Attorney General William Tong also criticized Character.ai’s business model. “Their chatbots drove vulnerable youth down a rabbit hole of emotionally volatile and sexually inappropriate chats,” Tong said . “Their reckless misconduct and broken business model drove their company into the ground. Now they want to abuse the bankruptcy process to do exactly what they said they wouldn’t do — auction off those private chat records and personal details to a shady buyer.” Tong added: “We objected to the Disney sale, and we’re calling on the bankruptcy court to reject this sale too as yet another guise to eviscerate legal liability and consumer protection.” The opposition to the Disney sale was led by a similar but not identical coalition of state AGs. They fought against a proposed $20 million licensing deal that would give Disney access to Character.ai’s intellectual property, but not to users’ chats. The deal has not yet received final court approval. (Disney also agreed to hire most of Character.ai’s remaining staff .) Character.ai suffered after its co-founders, Noam Shazeer and Daniel De Freitas, returned to Google , when the tech giant signed a non-exclusive license to use the AI startup’s tech. The company also faced lawsuits related to child safety — one involved the suicide of a 14-year-old Florida boy whose mother claimed he had become obsessed with a chatbot on the platform. California AG Bonta is joined in the effort to oppose the sale of Character.ai user data by attorneys general from Alaska, Arkansas, Colorado, Connecticut, the District of Columbia, Delaware, Florida, Georgia, Hawaii, Idaho, Illinois, Indiana, Kansas, Kentucky, Louisiana, Maine, Maryland, Michigan, Minnesota, Mississippi, Missouri, Nevada, New Hampshire, New Jersey, New York, North Carolina, North Dakota, Ohio, Oklahoma, Oregon, Pennsylvania, Rhode Island, South Carolina, South Dakota, Tennessee, Utah, Virginia, Vermont, Washington, Wisconsin, and West Virginia.

title: AI data centers are becoming harder to build, and neoclouds are feeling it
abstract: Listen on Apple Podcasts Listen on Spotify ⁠Nvidia has made clear⁠ it won’t backstop an AI data center until it’s nearly ready to run, and that’s landing just as neoclouds report construction delays and more expensive debt. The message to developers is that land, power, and a finished building matter more than a pitch deck. ⁠Anita Verma-Lallian⁠ has been selling exactly that. Her company, Arizona Land Consulting, assembles data center sites for developers, hyperscalers, AI labs, and neoclouds, giving her a view into who’s buying, what makes a site viable, and where projects are running into trouble. She also partners with investor ⁠Chamath Palihapitiya,⁠ who has been predicting an industry shakeout. On this episode of TechCrunch’s ⁠Equity⁠ podcast, Rebecca Bellan talks with Verma-Lallian about who bears the risk when Nvidia gets pickier, why speculative projects could be the first to fall apart, and what a 2027 shakeout might look like. Listen to the full episode to hear more about: What “land, power, shell” means, and why having all three could give some developers a major advantage. How community opposition and state-level restrictions are making some markets harder to build in than others. Utilities getting major customers like TSMC to help fund the infrastructure needed to deliver more power. Who gets stuck with the bill when a data center project stalls, from developers to lenders to customers. Why AI labs and hyperscalers might increasingly build their own data centers instead of relying on neoclouds. Who could benefit from a 2027 shakeout, including the companies best positioned to acquire distressed projects. Subscribe to Equity on ⁠YouTube⁠ , ⁠Apple Podcasts⁠ , ⁠Overcast⁠ , ⁠Spotify⁠ , and all the casts. You can also follow Equity on ⁠X⁠ and ⁠Threads⁠ , at @EquityPod.

title: Amazon and Meta reportedly in talks to lift blockade on AI agent Muse
abstract: Amazon may be having a change of heart about Meta’s AI agent, Muse. The two tech giants are reportedly discussing a potential deal that would allow Meta’s popular AI agent to connect directly to Amazon’s store. The talks would mark a significant reversal from just two months ago, when Muse users discovered they were unable to purchase products on Amazon and instead received an error message when attempting to check out. According to a Wednesday report by Fortune , citing people familiar with the discussions, Amazon and Meta have held multiple rounds of talks about the matter. Two key issues remain under negotiation: how search results would be presented and how advertising would be handled under a potential agreement. One of Amazon’s biggest concerns is how third-party shopping agents like Muse could affect its advertising business. In October, Amazon CEO Andy Jassy argued that few customers were making purchases through outside shopping agents. Amazon may also have been waiting for Muse to mature before agreeing to integrate it with its marketplace. If Muse places the wrong order or creates a problem with a purchase, Amazon could ultimately be left dealing with frustrated customers and unhappy sellers. Fortune reported that executives are concerned that third-party shopping agents could weaken Amazon’s direct relationship with consumers, according to people familiar with the matter. Any potential agreement between Amazon and Meta would reportedly require approval from both companies’ CEOs, Fortune also reported. Meta and Amazon have not yet responded to TechCrunch’s requests for comment.

title: The questions Jensen Huang and Nvidia will still have to answer about Megaspeed
abstract: Jensen Huang’s return as CEO to Nvidia hasn’t eased the scrutiny the company faces. The chipmaker still needs to address multiple inquiries into allegations that its advanced GPUs were smuggled into China by a customer, the Singapore-based data center operator Megaspeed, in violation of U.S. export rules designed to slow China’s development of frontier AI models. The central question for investigators is what Nvidia knew about where those chips ended up and whether Huang’s affair with a Megaspeed executive gave the company reason to doubt Megaspeed’s assurances. Huang’s return doesn’t settle that. U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche has suggested Nvidia isn’t a target of an investigation, but California’s attorney general and Congress are pressing ahead, and the Securities and Exchange Commission is reportedly investigating, too. The U.S. government opened an investigation into Megaspeed in 2024 and requested information from Nvidia about its billions of dollars in sales to the company, concerned that some of the chips Megaspeed bought for data center projects in Malaysia were in fact being diverted to China. Singapore also began investigating similar allegations in 2025. Megaspeed has denied any wrongdoing. Diversion of this kind would be a fairly routine issue for a company like Nvidia, whose in-demand chips are the targets of smugglers and resellers. When it comes to compliance and liability for export-control violations, Nvidia and other chip sellers need assurances that the end users of their chips are obeying the rules. However, they also cannot ignore other information that might call the reliability of those assurances into question, export-control attorneys told TechCrunch. And that’s why Jensen Huang’s affair with Megaspeed executive Alice Huang was such a problem for Nvidia, likely even more so than her alleged role as a source for Chinese intelligence agencies. If Nvidia personnel, from lower-level employees up to the CEO, had reason to believe that statements from Megaspeed weren’t reliable, the attorneys said, that would increase the company’s legal risk. “Government investigators likely would want to know, notwithstanding whatever formal assurances were exchanged between the parties, what anyone at Nvidia actually knew about the end use and end users of the chips,” Dan Fisher-Owens, an attorney at the firm Berliner Corcoran & Rowe, told TechCrunch last week. The concern Nvidia’s board faced when it decided to oust Huang is that he knew more about what Megaspeed was doing with Nvidia’s products than was reflected in any of the compliance statements. The Wall Street Journal reported that Alice Huang and her husband, Kang Wei, were part of a network of businesses that funneled chips to a company in Shanghai. Kang also reportedly introduced his wife to Jensen Huang, whom he had known for a decade. On Monday, the U.S. government added Megaspeed and its affiliates to a list of companies restricted from U.S. trade due to national security concerns. The U.S. also issued new rules last week barring large data centers that purchase U.S. chips from serving customers in China and other nations seen as problematic by the U.S. government. Nvidia, meanwhile, said it would stop selling licensed chips to China and laid out plans to hire its first compliance officer and create a new board committee focused on export controls. Nvidia’s board said it reinstated Huang on Monday after receiving “input from senior levels of the United States government” that left it confident his return posed no national security risk. President Donald Trump later said he called into the meeting to give them that assurance. In a news conference Tuesday, Blanche said that Nvidia was “a good corporate citizen” and suggested it is not the target of an investigation, but Blanche declined to answer questions about the government’s investigation into Megaspeed, which the Justice Department said was ongoing as recently as last week. “When you say the export investigation is still ongoing, I don’t know what you’re talking about,” Blanche said. Other authorities may be more demanding. Nvidia faces investigations by California Attorney General Rob Bonta and, reportedly , the SEC, both tied to its corporate disclosures. While many details of the investigation still aren’t known, short sellers complained about the company’s decision to stop breaking out its exports to Singapore in financial filings after journalists raised concerns about chip diversion. Members of Congress from both parties say they want answers from Nvidia, with many citing alarm about China and some questioning the White House’s role in Huang’s return. Three committees in the House of Representatives will privately interview Huang and Nvidia’s top lawyer, Tim Teter, next week. Teter reportedly intervened in the Department of Commerce’s investigation of Megaspeed last year. “We remain committed to getting answers on the mass smuggling of Nvidia products, their diversion for Chinese military purposes, and their key role in advancing our foremost adversary’s AI capabilities,” the Republican chairs of House committees focused on foreign affairs, intelligence, and China said in a joint statement. Rep. Brian Mast, the chair of the House Foreign Affairs Committee, has also demanded that the Department of Commerce share extensive data regarding its investigation into chip smuggling, including by Megaspeed and its affiliates. The Senate Banking Committee will also question Huang in a public hearing on December 3. “Mr. Huang, Nvidia executives, and the company’s board still owe Congress answers about the company’s compliance with U.S. export controls,” Senator Elizabeth Warren, the ranking Democratic member on the committee, said in a statement. “The Trump Administration also needs to explain to Congress what ‘input’ was given and by which senior officials in the United States government to support his reinstatement.”

title: Google’s patent for custom AI video feeds paints a bleak picture of entertainment’s future
abstract: Entertainment AI Streaming Google’s patent for custom AI video feeds paints a bleak picture of entertainment’s future Imagine an endless feed of AI slop in which you are the main character of every story.﻿ Imagine an endless feed of AI slop in which you are the main character of every story.﻿ by Charles Pulliam-Moore Nov 25, 2026, 9:51 PM UTC Image: Google Charles Pulliam-Moore is a reporter focusing on film, TV, and pop culture. Before The Verge, he wrote about comic books, labor, race, and more at io9 and Gizmodo for almost five years. Last year, Google filed a patent for a system called My Channel that’s designed to create feeds filled with personalized, AI-generated videos and advertisements based on information the company knows about its users. The patent has been rejected, but unfortunately, Google might appeal or resubmit an amended version, and we could see this monstrosity come to market. First spotted by Patentlyze , the patent — which was filed last May and published last week — describes how My Channel would use a person’s demographic data and viewing history to create its own prompts that would then be fed into an LLM to help generate AI videos tailored to that person’s specific interests. In addition to factoring in what kinds of videos a user tends to watch, the system would capture contextual data from their device like IP addresses, GPS locations, and specific details about the user’s age. My Channel could also base its prompts on current news like sports scores and things happening on social media, and all of the video generation would take place on Google’s servers. According to the patent, My Channel would be able to churn out entire movies of various genres. If a user watches a lot of videos about Christopher Nolan’s The Odyssey , the system might serve up something like Ash Koosha’s Odysseus: The Fall . The patent details how My Channel might be able to connect to other streaming services — which would give it even more information about users and, presumably, access to useful training data for video generation. It all seems like a convoluted way to whip up AI knockoffs of professionally produced art, but what’s most unsettling about the patent are its mentions of My Channel creating digital avatars of users and turning them into “the protagonist or lead character” in the content it pumps out. Image: Google Setting aside the fact that My Channel would use photos, videos, and audio clips of people to create these avatars, the system sounds like it is designed to generate a form of “entertainment” that is deeply at odds with what makes engaging with art a worthwhile, enjoyable experience. It can be fun to metaphorically project one’s self into fictional narratives to understand how characters feel, but what Google is proposing is giving people access to an endless supply of bespoke content that doesn’t at all encourage them to use their imaginations to empathize with or relate to the characters. The patent makes it seem like Google thinks that viewers would be entertained enough just by seeing themselves onscreen. That’s bleak in and of itself because My Channel sounds very much like an unholy cross between JibJab and the panoptic elements of Google. My Channel feels like an even more depressing idea when you consider how the service would make it that much easier for its users to avoid broadening their horizons by being exposed to new things that exist outside their comfort zones. If Google were able to strike the right licensing deals with other streaming services, My Channel users could presumably gorge themselves on artless AI regurgitations of preexisting content. That might keep some people glued to the service — a goal that every streaming platform strives for — but it would also discourage them from engaging with entertainment that isn’t expressly crafted to appeal to their assumed tastes. When people refer to AI-generated videos as “slop,” they’re talking about the fact that generative models are incapable of generating art with the same kind of creative intention that makes human-made stories compelling. Video generation models can mimic visual elements of the data (read: movies and series) they’re trained on, but they cannot truly think or feel in the way that directors, writers, and actors can. This reality is why it has been so baffling to see AI-boosting entertainment companies, streamers, and studios insisting that the technology will fundamentally revolutionize the industry for the better. It feels much more likely that gen AI is going to keep flooding the internet with garbage no one wants to watch. title: FCC signs off on SpaceX’s plan to put up to 1 million data center satellites into space
abstract: Science AI News FCC signs off on SpaceX’s plan to put up to 1 million data center satellites into space SpaceX aims to power AI capabilities here on Earth with its ‘Starmind’ constellation. SpaceX aims to power AI capabilities here on Earth with its ‘Starmind’ constellation. by Emma Roth Nov 25, 2026, 5:44 PM UTC Photo by Mario Tama/Getty Images Emma Roth is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more. Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO. In an announcement on Wednesday , the FCC says it authorized SpaceX to deploy up to 1 million AI chip-equipped satellites as part of the Elon Musk-owned company’s “Starmind” initiative . With several others also pursuing the idea of putting AI data centers in space , including Google and Blue Origin, this is the first approval the agency has granted for a full “constellation” of AI satellites. The FCC’s approval requires SpaceX to deploy at least one satellite by 2033, and meet the 1 million satellite milestone by 2040. The FCC also deferred SpaceX’s request to dispose of satellites located above 600km in space “graveyard” orbits , rather than having them burn up in the Earth’s atmosphere, saying the company hasn’t provided “sufficient information” about its disposal process plans. SpaceX has described its Starmind project as a way to “capture solar energy in space to power” AI capabilities on Earth. The company says Starmind will transmit data to Earth using high-speed lasers that connect to Starlink. It plans to produce chips for its satellites at an upcoming Terafab facility . Google has already taken its first steps toward putting compute into space, with the launch of a “Project Suncatcher” AI server satellite last month. Jeff Bezos’ Blue Origin will carry out the first dedicated heavy-lift launch for Project Suncatcher in 2029. title: Nothing offers a full look at its AI earbuds and charging case
abstract: Gadgets AI News Nothing offers a full look at its AI earbuds and charging case The Ear Note buds look similar to Nothing’s previous earbuds, but now their case doubles as an AI-connected note taker for conversations. The Ear Note buds look similar to Nothing’s previous earbuds, but now their case doubles as an AI-connected note taker for conversations. by Emma Roth Nov 25, 2026, 4:00 PM UTC Image: Nothing Emma Roth is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more. Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO. Nothing is showing off a much more detailed look at its upcoming AI earbuds ahead of their December 8th release. The Ear Note buds can record your calls, while their charging case can record, transcribe, and summarize your conversations. Like the Ear 3 , the Ear Note’s microphone-equipped case comes with a “Talk” button that you can use to record your own voice. There’s also a new “Record” button that can record and transcribe your conversations. In a post on X , Nothing CEO Carl Pei says the button will allow you to record calls through the earbuds, and meetings through the case as a “first step toward a hardware context layer for AI.” As previously reported by Bloomberg , the buds will connect to an app where you can manage recordings, transcriptions, and AI summaries. They’ll also “support interactions with various AI agents, including a more basic voice-control system developed by Nothing, letting users engage in back-and-forth conversations,” according to Bloomberg . The Ear Note buds themselves look similar to the Ear 3 and Ear 3A, but come with Nothing’s “best in-ear audio to date.” The new device, which Nothing teased earlier this month , will join some of the other AI-powered note-taking devices we’ve seen emerge recently, such as the Amazon Bee and the Plaud Note Pro . Apple also brought AI capabilities to its Watch Series 12, allowing Siri to listen to your conversations and generate recaps. title: Amazon is reportedly in talks to end Muse AI shopping block
abstract: Tech AI News Amazon is reportedly in talks to end Muse AI shopping block Amazon is concerned that Muse AI could have an impact on its advertising revenue, according to Fortune. Amazon is concerned that Muse AI could have an impact on its advertising revenue, according to Fortune. by Emma Roth Nov 25, 2026, 2:12 PM UTC Image: The Verge, Getty Images, Meta Part Of All the latest news on Meta’s cute, creepy Muse AI agent see all updates Emma Roth is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more. Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO. Amazon has held talks about letting Meta’s Muse AI agent shop on its online marketplace, according to a report from Fortune . The discussions, which could end Amazon’s block on Muse , reportedly center on the kinds of products the AI agent recommends and the potential impact on the ecommerce giant’s advertising revenue. As reported by Fortune , Amazon is concerned that it could lose advertising revenue by allowing Muse on its site, since it depends on actual humans seeing ads across its online marketplace. It’s also reportedly worried about the quality of the product search results that Muse will present to users, as well as whether the AI agent will affect Amazon’s relationship with customers. Neither Amazon nor Meta immediately responded to The Verge ’s request for comment. Though some online retailers, such as Walmart, Best Buy, Gap, and Sephora, have opened their digital doors to AI agents like Muse, Amazon has been more hesitant. Amazon also blocked Perplexity’s AI agent from shopping on its site, and has instead focused on promoting its own Alexa for Shopping assistant , which customers can now text to shop on their behalf . title: Has vibe coding made open source the new normal for synths?
abstract: AI Tech Has vibe coding made open source the new normal for synths? Companies like Akai have decided to embrace the modding community rather than resist vibe coders. by Terrence O'Brien Nov 25, 2026, 1:00 PM UTC Image: The Verge; Adobe Stock Terrence O'Brien is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths. The emergence of powerful vibe-coding agents and tools like Reverse Engineer Anything has caused chaos in the music gear world , leaving companies scrambling to figure out how to respond. While some, like Roland, have remained silent for now, others have embraced the modding community. In the last several weeks, as it’s become clear that no piece of music gear is safe from Claude and a subreddit full of curious tinkerers, companies have begun making more and more of their devices open source. The biggest name to decide “if you can’t beat ’em, join ’em” is inMusic , the parent company of Akai, Moog, Native Instruments, and more. “We’re going to provide a toolbox to the community, we’re going to provide the inner workings of, say, an MPC or Sample so that people can do what they want,” inMusic CEO Jack O’Donnell tells The Verge . That includes a recently launched SDK and several open-source devices, including the recently teased MPC Sample Key . Akai is trying to walk a fine line, offering modders access while keeping its products reliable for professionals. O’Donnell says the company will “try to give them a reset button” so “they can experiment with it, and then not lose what they have.” Behringer has also rushed to cash in, announcing a slew of open-source devices. In just a matter of weeks, it announced a $150 clone of the MPC One called Kick , a clone of the E-mu SP-1200 , the Anima DJ controller , the Ignite sequencer, and the Polykeys 61 MIDI controller, all of which are open source. It’s unclear when any of these products might launch. M-Vave’s FM-1 helped kick-start the whole movement. The $70 pocketable clone of the iconic Yamaha DX7 became the synth of the summer not just because of its dirt-cheap price and faithfully re-created ’80s tones, but because it also turned out to be infinitely hackable. There are well over a dozen different custom firmwares for the FM-1. M-Vave responded by releasing an open-source firmware with more features for developers to build on. The company also confirmed that a successor, the FM-2, is in development and will be open source as well. Other companies have also embraced the modding community. Erica Synths recently released the source code for its LXR-02 drum machine , but founder Ģirts Ozoliņš isn’t necessarily fully on board with vibe coding. “Inventions succeed if they solve some fundamental problems, right?” he tells The Verge . “So, I’m still wondering what fundamental problem vibe coding solves.” “We’re going to provide a toolbox to the community.” While he can’t imagine a producer simply stacking his studio with a bunch of hacked FM-1s running various synth engines, he’s curious to see what the community cooks up for the LXR. And he does see a benefit in making music tech a little less disposable. “What I like on the upside of this is that there is some trace of sustainability. Instead of buying five or 10 plastic boxes, you can try options on one,” he says, though he’s under no illusions about the environmental impact of vibe coding. “Of course it by far does not offset data center impact on the planet and on ecology and stuff like that.” Polyend has also gotten on board, open-sourcing its line of Tracker grooveboxes. The Polish company’s decision to open its arms to vibe coders isn’t too much of a surprise. Last year it released the Endless guitar pedal, which lets users vibe-code their own effects. Opening its other instruments to AI tinkering feels like a natural extension. Elektron is less thrilled about the emergence of vibe-coded mods. The company banned links to custom firmware from its official forums, saying, “We would always warn against modifications to our firmware and/or machines that could brick them (potentially rendering them unusable), prevent future updates, affect warranty coverage.” Elektron’s CPO Christian Alsing told YouTuber EZBOT that he was sympathetic to the hacker community and that the company has roots there with its first instrument, the Sidstation (based on the iconic SID sound chip from the Commodore 64). He also said that he believes users have a right to modify their devices as they see fit. But he pushed back on the idea that Elektron is “withholding features,” an accusation that Akai also faced . Ģirts also defended Elektron, saying, “people tend to blame the company, saying they are hiding features ... you design an instrument, you have a specific concept in mind, and you cannot foresee millions of possibilities ... it’s not about hiding features; it’s more about having an idea of how an instrument should look and work.” Other major music manufacturers, like Roland, Korg, Arturia, and Novation – all of whom did not comment for this story – have yet to issue any public statements about the explosion of AI-aided custom firmwares. title: Where scientists draw the line on AI agents
abstract: Back to Articles Where scientists draw the line on AI agents Enterprise Article Published November 25, 2026 Upvote 5 Kyle Wiggers Ai2Comms Follow allenai 📄 Tech Report Delegating research tasks to AI does not remove scientists’ responsibility for how the work is accomplished. For example, a researcher using AI to review the literature needs to check whether the system overlooks conflicting evidence or makes claims the cited papers don’t support. Someone handing off data analysis to an agentic system needs to understand which methods it used, which files it accessed, and whether the results can be successfully reproduced. A researcher automating part of a lab protocol needs confidence that the system respects physical safety constraints, such as temperature limits or material toxicity, while a researcher working with human-participant data needs assurance that a system protects participants' privacy and limits who can access their information. Researchers also need clear institutional guidelines for verifying and disclosing AI-assisted work. These ethical and safety questions are central to our work on AI for science. Responsible science is about more than accuracy—scientific fields have ethical research norms because of past actions and choices by scientists and scientific communities, and those norms also cover how research is conducted and what impact it has. We want AI tools to expand what scientists can accomplish without compromising their ability to scrutinize evidence, verify methods, and – perhaps most importantly – stand behind their findings. To better understand what that requires, we interviewed 17 scientists working in the natural, applied, and social sciences about the responsible development of AI agents. These systems can use tools and carry out research tasks with varying degrees of autonomy. The interviews drew on a network of researchers established through earlier survey work—we wanted to understand how scientists would steer AI’s development to reflect the responsibilities of their fields. We asked where researchers would welcome agentic assistance, what could go wrong, and what safeguards they would need to trust agents with their own studies. Our interest in these questions grew out of work to evaluate the safety of models developed at Ai2. As we expand our focus on AI for science, we’ve found that much of the safety work on scientific applications emphasizes catastrophic risks in areas such as biology and nuclear physics. We also need ways to assess whether agents follow the standards of responsible conduct of research in the fields where they’re used. One of our main findings concerns trust. Across the interviews, we identified five dimensions of scientific trust : validation, privacy, objectivity, accountability, and transparency. Together, they reflect concerns that go beyond whether an AI system produces a correct answer. Researchers also need to understand how an answer was reached, protect sensitive information, recognize bias, and determine who is charged with verifying and standing behind AI-assisted findings. These are matters of responsible conduct of research. Another main finding suggests that scientists should help decide which research tasks agents take on, how those agents operate, and how their performance is evaluated. Even a technically correct result may be unsuitable for scientific use if researchers cannot inspect how it was produced, or if an agent accesses confidential data or files beyond what the researcher authorized. A third key finding pertains to the future of science. Interviewees were divided between excitement about AI-driven progress and existential concern about the role of human scientists. They proposed training in AI use and named developing and enforcing guidelines as a critical, timely challenge. Helping researchers check the work For many participants in our interviews, the appeal of AI agents began with time-consuming research tasks—processing large datasets, writing code, documenting experimental procedures, and handling repetitive administrative work. Automating these activities could free researchers to spend more time on fieldwork, mentoring, or developing new ideas. It could also make it possible to analyze volumes of data that would be difficult to examine manually. But delegating research tasks creates a corresponding need to verify the work an AI system performs. Several participants described checking AI-generated answers against original publications rather than accepting summaries at face value. They worried about confident responses containing subtle inaccuracies, as well as tools that reinforce assumptions by retrieving only studies that support a favored hypothesis. But checking the final answer from an AI system is only part of the challenge. Researchers may also need to know which sources an agent omitted, whether it followed the requested methodology, and what information it accessed along the way. Our interviews suggest how evaluations of AI agents for scientific research could better reflect these concerns. A literature-review benchmark, for example, could test whether an agent overlooks contradictory evidence or draws conclusions unsupported by its sources. A coding benchmark could assess not only whether the generated code works, but whether the agent accesses files outside its authorized scope. Evaluations of data-processing agents could compare their methods and results with established human workflows. These examples point toward a longer-term goal—a participatory benchmark in which scientists help define the research practices and safety requirements that agents should be tested against. We want to evaluate whether systems developed at Ai2 or elsewhere follow the standards of the fields where they’re used, as well as whether they complete assigned tasks. These evaluations remain proposals to develop and test with scientists, rather than established solutions. But they offer a direction for our work at Ai2: building open scientific tools means making their behavior and limitations easier to investigate and giving the research community a role in defining what trustworthy performance looks like. Keep scientific judgment in the loop Verification is only one consideration in using AI tools for science. Respondents also raised a more fundamental question—what happens to scientific expertise when AI takes over parts of the research process? An early-career biologist described deliberately limiting AI use while acquiring skills they hoped to teach future students. Another researcher questioned whether producing a correct result was sufficient if the researcher learned nothing in the process: even with perfect outputs, “did the person who obtained the perfect outputs get anything out of this?” Some participants were concerned that AI-assisted research could diminish learning, though the value of automation depends in part on the researcher and the task. An experienced scientist may reasonably delegate a familiar procedure to save time, while someone still learning that procedure may benefit from doing the work themselves. Participants also drew different boundaries around activities involving intellectual contribution. One biologist refused to use AI to generate research ideas, considering that a responsibility to retain personally. Others were more open to AI-assisted ideation or writing. An anthropologist, for example, argued that some sections of scientific papers, particularly routine descriptions of methods and results, are formulaic enough to benefit from automation. Even researchers who tried AI for writing sometimes reconsidered. One political scientist described using Claude to help revise a manuscript, then deciding to rewrite the entire paper because the boundaries of their own intellectual contribution had become unclear. “I don’t know what was AI and what was me,” the researcher said. Context mattered, too.

title: An Indic Voice Agent with CUGA
abstract: Back to Articles An Indic Voice Agent with CUGA Enterprise Article Published November 25, 2026 Upvote 7 +1 Vrunda Gadesha vrunda-gadesha Follow ibm-research Cyril Shaji cyrilshaji Follow ibm-research Jobit Treesa Varughese jotreesa1 Follow ibm-research Nivetha Suruliraj nivetha-suruliraj Follow ibm-research Anu Sugunan anu24-hugface Follow ibm-research Anupama Murthi anupamamurthi Follow ibm-research Jaydeep Sen JaydeepSen Follow ibm-research Amith Singhee asinghee Follow ibm-research Most useful knowledge is written and digitized in English. Most of the people who need it speak, and think, in their own regional languages like Hindi, Tamil, Telugu, Gujarati, Marathi and many others. Many would rather talk than type. We built a small voice agent to close that gap, using CUGA as the agent harness. This post explains the use case and what we learned. You can try it yourself in CUGA Apps . The use case: a Farm Assistant A farmer asks a question aloud, in their own language: how do I tell good seed from bad? The agent: Listens and turns the speech into text. Searches a 154-page agricultural handbook, which is written in English. Answers in two to four spoken sentences, in the language the question was asked in, using only what the handbook says. Speaks the answer back and shows the source pages, so the answer can be checked. If someone asks about cricket or coding, it politely steers them back to farming instead of making something up. Where CUGA fits CUGA (ConfigUrable Generalist Agent) is IBM Research's open-source agent harness. It handles the model wiring, tool management, state and guardrails, so you write tools and a prompt instead of the agent loop. Here we use it as an embedded SDK inside a small web app, for three things: One agent, any model. Switch between watsonx and OpenAI with one setting. The knowledge engine. Parse a PDF, chunk it, embed it, and search it locally with agent.knowledge.search() . Conversation threads. Each question gets a fresh thread, so one person's language or context never leaks into another's. The key design idea is simple: CUGA is a text-in, text-out brain. Voice is two thin layers around it. audio ──▶ speech-to-text ──▶ knowledge.search ──▶ CUGA (grounded answer) ──▶ text-to-speech ──▶ audio Because the agent only ever sees text, you can build and test it with plain text first, then add the ears and the mouth. You can also swap speech providers without touching the agent. We support two: Sarvam AI's cloud speech APIs, called directly from the user's browser, and open-source models (SraVaani for speech-to-text, Svara for text-to-speech) running on your own server. The hard part is not the voice Adding speech is the easy part. The hard part is cross-lingual retrieval : a Hindi question has to find an English paragraph. Search works by turning text into vectors and finding the nearest ones. CUGA's default embedding model is English-only, so it turns Hindi into vectors that carry almost no meaning. With it, a Hindi or Tamil question still retrieves five passages, but they are the wrong ones. The model, correctly told to answer only from what it was given, quietly says "the handbook doesn't cover that". Every layer behaves correctly, so there is no error and no warning. The fix is to use a multilingual embedding model (we use intfloat/multilingual-e5-large ), so the same meaning lands in the same place whatever the language. Conceptually simple, though wiring it into CUGA took a small workaround (shown in the tutorial). After that, one English document serves every language, and you do not need translated copies of anything. Our advice: before you tune a single prompt, ask your agent one question in a non-English language and check that it finds the right pages. Making it sound right and keeping it safe A few small decisions mattered more than we expected: Write for the ear. Markdown, bullet points, citation tags and bracketed translations such as "millet (बाजरा)" all sound wrong when read aloud. The prompt asks the model not to produce them, and a light formatter strips any that slip through before speech. Keep guardrails cheap. Simple input checks catch obvious off-topic questions. If one gets through, the model starts its reply with OFF_TOPIC , and the app swaps in a polite redirect. No second LLM call, so the voice path stays fast. Ground every answer. The model sees only the retrieved passages, is told not to use outside knowledge, and the page sources are shown to the user. Keep keys out of the server. With the Sarvam option, the browser talks to Sarvam directly. The server receives only text and never sees the user's key. Try it You do not need to set anything up to see it work. Open the voice agent in CUGA Apps on Hugging Face Spaces, ask a farming question in your language, and listen to the answer: CUGA Apps on Hugging Face → Want to build one yourself? Our step-by-step tutorial, Build an Indic Voice Agent with CUGA , starts from an empty folder and adds each layer in turn. Beyond farming: Scaling for Bharat Nothing here is specific to agriculture. Swap the handbook for scheme documents, health advisories, or legal guides, and you have a different assistant. Swap the speech provider and you change the deployment model, such as cloud for speed or on-premises for data sovereignty, without rewriting the agent. Voice-first, multilingual assistants are how digital services can reach people who were never served well by English-only text screens. Building them on an open, auditable harness, with answers tied to sources people can check, is how they earn trust. This approach sits precisely at the intersection of what we are building with IBM Bharat Core. Bharat Core is an optimized AI stack built on top of IBM Sovereign Core, designed specifically for the Indian ecosystem to run Indic AI workloads securely on local infrastructure. When scaling a voice agent from a prototype to a secure enterprise application (like a vernacular KYC system or multilingual government bot), you need greater control over data sovereignty. By pairing CUGA’s flexible agent harness with Bharat Core’s ready-to-deploy Indic connectors and fine-tuned models, developers can build fully compliant, sovereign AI solutions tailored to India's unique linguistic diversity. If you are building for India at scale, see the work happening at IBM Bharat Core . Learn more about CUGA New to CUGA? Here are some places to start: cuga.dev : the CUGA home page. CUGA on GitHub : the open-source harness (Apache 2.0). Star it, file issues, or pick up a good first issue. CUGA documentation : setup, the SDK, knowledge, policies and configuration. CUGA Apps gallery on GitHub : the source for the apps in the Hugging Face Space. Spaces you can try in your browser: CUGA Agent : the general-purpose agent, running on a demo CRM scenario. CUGA Apps : launch working CUGA apps from one dashboard. CUGA Policy Playground : two live agents side by side, one with policies and one without. More CUGA posts on the Hugging Face blog: CUGA on Hugging Face: Democratizing Configurable AI Agents : the introduction to CUGA and its configurable reasoning modes. Build real agentic apps using CUGA: two dozen working examples on a lightweight harness : the app gallery this voice agent belongs to. Same Model, Different Harness: CUGA, Hermes, and Deep Agents — When to Pick CUGA? : how much the harness matters when the model stays the same.

title: Hill-climbing Inkling 2 Mini inference on one RTX PRO 6000
abstract:
Back to Articles Hill-climbing Inkling 2 Mini inference on one RTX PRO 6000 Published November 25, 2026 Update on GitHub Upvote 2 Niels Rogge nielsr Follow Inkling 2 Mini came out last week and sets a new state of the art for local AI and smaller open-source models. With ~26B total parameters (3B active per token), multimodal inputs, and a 1M-token context window, it leads its weight class on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v5 and across 32 of 48 benchmarks against models like Gemma 4 31B and Qwen3.8-27B, making it a strong open option for coding, tool use, and reasoning on modest hardware. We wrote an extensive blog post on how you can use it within the Hugging Face ecosystem here . One of the interesting aspects of Inkling 2 Mini that might explain its great performance is its unusual architecture. Inkling 2 Mini is a looped Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model with 24 physical layers where the middle 12 layers run three times, so every token passes through 48 layers. The checkpoint ships in mixed NVFP4 and MXFP8 and bundles a DSpark drafter for speculative decoding. Both vLLM and SGLang, the go-to frameworks for LLM inference, support it on nightly builds, though the published serving recipes target NVIDIA B200 and GB300 GPUs ( sm100 ), leaving out sm120 cards like the NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 where kernel compatibility can differ. We wanted to see how fast we could serve it on a single NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 96 GB, the GPU behind an nvidia-rtx-pro-6000 Inference Endpoint . Rather than tuning flags by hand, we gave a coding agent the inference-optimisation skill, the hf CLI, and access to Hugging Face Jobs , and let it run experiments for an afternoon. Across 46 valid benchmark runs, single-user decode went from 136 to 190.6 tok/s (+40%) (ahead of the 167.7 tok/s community SGLang + DSpark benchmark on LocalMaxxing for the same GPU) and 8-user aggregate throughput went from ~570 to 716 tok/s (+26%) using vLLM nightly with DSpark speculative decoding. Greedy outputs are byte-identical with and without speculation, long-context needle retrieval passes 3/3 up to 250K tokens, and the winning config is now running as an Inference Endpoint from a pinned image digest. All logs, scripts, and raw measurements are in NielsRogge/inkling-2-mini-hillclimb . The setup The inference-optimisation skill gives an agent a fixed experimental protocol and a small, engine-agnostic benchmark script ( bench.py ): Measure the hardware and estimate theoretical ceilings before tuning. Change one variable at a time and bracket every candidate between two control runs ( control → candidate → control ). Keep a change only if it beats both controls without regressing other metrics. Log every run in PLAN.md , including regressions and dead ends. Pass long-context, concurrency, and greedy-equivalence checks before declaring a winner. bench.py measures single-user decode, aggregate decode at concurrency N, cold prefill at several lengths, and TTFT, using token counts directly from the server's usage response. All runs used a fixed panel of six prompts (code, an explanation, a story, a comparison table, a bash script, and a history summary) at temperature 1.0 (the model's default), thinking on, 512 output tokens, and 12 repetitions whenever speculative decoding was enabled. The skill was written for a local GPU, so we adapted it to Hugging Face infrastructure: HF Jobs for compute. The rtx-pro-6000 Job flavor uses the same GPU as the nvidia-rtx-pro-6000 Inference Endpoint ($2.75/h for both), so Job numbers transfer directly. A ~150-line driver ( jobs/driver.py ) takes a list of server configs, starts each one, runs an unmeasured warmup, calls bench.py unmodified, shuts the server down, and prints one ledger line per run. Because Jobs run on separate machines, the agent swept SGLang ( lmsysorg/sglang:inkling-2-mini ) and vLLM nightly ( vllm/vllm-openai:nightly ) in parallel. CPU Jobs for reading engine source. When a flag was undocumented, the agent ran a cheap cpu-upgrade Job to grep the installed Python package inside the container. That is how it found SGLang's SGLANG_OPT_* environment variables and vLLM's speculative-config fields. Inference Endpoints for deployment, created via hf endpoints deploy using the exact image digest and flags that passed verification. The baseline was our existing org endpoint config: SGLang with --attention-backend fa4 and no speculative decoding. Results Single-user decode speed (median of 12 requests). vLLM + DSpark reaches ~95% of the memory-bandwidth ceiling at its measured acceptance rate. Config (1× RTX PRO 6000) 1-user decode (tok/s) 8-user aggregate (tok/s) Prefill 4K / 32K (tok/s) TTFT SGLang, no speculation (baseline) 134–139 543–598 18.7–19.1K / 16.9–19.1K 41–114 ms vLLM, no speculation 157.0 638 20.7K / 20.7K 33 ms SGLang + DSpark (8 drafts) 166.6 — ¹ 18.0–19.5K / 18.9–19.1K 38–51 ms vLLM + DSpark (7 drafts) 190.6 716 20.7K / 20.6K 40 ms Deployed endpoint (over the internet) 194.9 673 11.7K / 19.2K ² 198 ms ² ¹ SGLang's RTX PRO 6000 DSpark recipe caps --max-running-requests at 4. Raising it to 8 reached 660 tok/s, still behind vLLM.
² Includes ~160 ms of client-to-endpoint network round trip. All of the speedup comes from switching to vLLM nightly (+15% over SGLang without speculation, 136 → 157 tok/s), enabling DSpark with 7 drafts and probabilistic draft sampling (+21% on top, 157 → 190.6 tok/s across four runs: 189.3, 190.4, 191.1, and 190.7), and adding two memory flags so vLLM's DSpark setup actually starts on 96 GB: vllm serve thinkingmachines/Inkling-2-Mini \ --tool-call-parser inkling \ --enable-auto-tool-choice \ --reasoning-parser inkling \ --max-model-len 262144 \ --gpu-memory-utilization 0.85 \ --speculative-config '{"method":"dspark","num_speculative_tokens":7,"draft_sample_method":"probabilistic"}' Both num_speculative_tokens: 7 and draft_sample_method: "probabilistic" were validated directly: shorter draft counts (such as 5) are rejected at startup because both engines enforce the checkpoint's fixed block size, and switching to greedy draft sampling dropped vLLM decode speed by 11% at temperature 1.0 (see What didn't work ). Why it stops around 190 tok/s Before tuning, the agent probed the RTX PRO 6000 inside a Job ( 1,469 GB/s copy bandwidth, 416 TFLOPS BF16, 792 TFLOPS FP8) and read tensor sizes from the safetensors header. Because every token makes 48 layer visits, plain decode re-reads ~2.7 GB of attention and dense weights, ~2 GB of routed experts (8 of 128 per layer), and ~0.9 GB for the LM head. At 1,469 GB/s, that gives a single-user bandwidth ceiling of ~256 tok/s . Without speculation, vLLM at 157 tok/s hits 61% of that ceiling, mostly limited by kernel launch latency across 48 visits. Speculative decoding changes the memory math on an MoE. Verifying 8 positions together activates the union of their routed experts, reading roughly 40% of each layer's experts instead of 6%. At our measured acceptance of ~2.3 tokens per step at temperature 1.0 (per-position acceptance drops from 0.6 on the first draft to 0.33 and 0.19), the bandwidth ceiling falls to ~201 tok/s . At 190.6 tok/s, vLLM + DSpark is already at ~95% of hardware bandwidth , so further flag tuning has almost nowhere left to go. Moving past 190 tok/s would take a drafter with higher acceptance at temperature 1.0 or a verification path that touches fewer experts per layer. What didn't work Most candidate flags were unsupported, noisy, or slower: vLLM Lever Result Shorter draft length (3–6) Rejected at startup; requires num_speculative_tokens = 7 (checkpoint block size − 1). draft_sample_method: "greedy" −11% at temperature 1.0 (168.6 vs ~190.4 tok/s). rejection_sample_method: "block" 190.1 vs 190.3–190.5 for controls; no effect. enable_adaptive_verification Assertion error at startup for the Inkling 2 drafter. draft_lm_head_quantization: "fp8" Only supported for DeepSeek DSpark drafters.

title: ByteDance Researchers Open-Sources Laminar, an Async Reinforcement Learning RL Post-Training Framework
abstract: Researchers from The University of Hong Kong and ByteDance Seed have open-sourced Laminar . Laminar is an reinforcement learning RL post-training framework for LLMs and long-horizon agents. The core idea is simple: stop forcing every trajectory and every GPU to wait for the slowest one. For teams training coding agents with long, skewed rollouts, that is where most GPU time goes. Laminar is an asynchronous RL post-training framework that decouples rollout, buffering, training and weight transfer into independent loops. It is built on verl and Uni-Agent and released under Apache-2.0. The launch blog splits the stack into 3 layers. verl provides training and inference compute backends. Uni-Agent handles agent execution, tool calls and sandboxes. Laminar handles cluster-scale orchestration. The design rests on 3 principles: full decoupling, fine-grained asynchrony and fault tolerance. In the research paper , relays are CPU processes, 1 per rollout machine. They broadcast weights along a pipelined RDMA chain. A 72B model reaches 127 other relays in under 1.6 seconds. Most async systems use version-mixed partial rollout. They interrupt in-flight trajectories at each weight update and resume under the new policy. That forces repeated re-prefill. Laminar also supports a version-consistent mode. Each trajectory finishes under 1 policy version. Replicas update independently, without a global weight-switch barrier. The blog states that this keeps the prefix KV cache intact. It argues re-prefill cost scales cubically with sequence length under frequent updates. Repack handles the tail. Once new weights exist, leftover old-version trajectories are consolidated onto fewer replicas. Drained replicas then load the new version immediately. The research team trained Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B-Instruct on SWE-rebench. They evaluated on all 500 SWE-bench Verified tasks with greedy decoding. Faults stay local. If a rollout replica fails, the router fences only that replica. It restarts, reloads weights from the local relay and resumes from its generated token prefix. A replica that fails during weight loading recovers without blocking the trainer. Trainer checkpoints align model state, prompt cursors and published weight versions. laminar.eval also evaluates several checkpoints at once across resident replicas, in batch or streaming mode during training. Check out the Paper , arXiv preprint , GitHub Repo and Technical Blog . You can check the deployment options and specs here through our GPULeaderboard.com chrome extension .
